title: Fact-checking of political information about the Russo-Ukrainian conflict
screen_reason: Quantitative and qualitative content analysis of all 128 Snopes.com fact-checking reports on the Russo-Ukrainian conflict published 24 February 2022 - 28 June 2023. It reports a verdict distribution with a real denominator and a genuine mix of outcomes (not an all-false corpus): 54.7% of the 128 claims were rated invalid (False, Miscaptioned or Outdated) and 32.0% rated False outright, against 21.9% True. That is a share of items in a sample classified false, i.e. CONTENT. The denominator is nevertheless a fact-checker-curated selection, so the row is flagged borderline and coded denom_selection=curated / sampling_frame=curated_seed; it measures Snopes' selection and verdict practice, not the prevalence of falsehood in any population of content.

estimates.country: Not stated; claims concern the Russo-Ukrainian conflict and were checked by Snopes.com, a US fact-checking organisation, in English
estimates.platform: Snopes.com fact-check reports on claims circulating across social media (videos and photographs), newspapers, television and statements by government representatives
estimates.measure_type: % of Snopes fact-checks on the Russo-Ukrainian conflict whose rating indicated the claim was invalid (False, Miscaptioned or Outdated)
estimates.value_raw: 54.7% of 128 reports (Table 2: False 32.0 + Miscaptioned 21.1 + Outdated 1.6; the 54.7% total is printed by the author in the abstract and in Section 5.1)
estimates.denominator: 128 Snopes.com fact-checking reports on the Russo-Ukrainian conflict, i.e. every report returned by searching the site for 'Russia AND Ukraine' and 'Ukraine AND war' over the 16-month window
estimates.definition: A report counted in the numerator if Snopes assigned one of the three negatively coloured ratings: False (primary elements demonstrably false), Miscaptioned (a real photograph or video accompanied by explanatory material that falsely describes its origin, context or meaning) or Outdated (subsequent events have rendered the original truth rating irrelevant)
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper works from a definition of fact-checking rather than of misinformation: "the practice of systematically publishing assessments of the validity of claims made by public officials and institutions with an explicit attempt to identify whether a claim is factual" (Walter et al., 2020, p. 351), and treats the Snopes rating scale as the operational criterion of validity
estimates.source_quote: The share of negatively coloured assessments (False, Miscaptioned, and Outdated) indicative of the invalidity of the claims was 54.7%, while the share of positive ratings (True, Correct Attribution) was 26.7%. The share of mixed assessments was 15.6%.
estimates.page_loc: Section 5.1 'Quantitative overview', p. 86, with Table 2 'The percentage distribution of the ratings (n = 128)'; repeated in the Abstract and at Section 5.3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Ratings are Snopes.com's own, assigned by its professional fact-checkers using a 20-category scale (9 categories occur in this sample); the author only regrouped them into valid (True, Correct Attribution), invalid (False, Miscaptioned, Outdated) and mixed (Mixture, Labelled Satire, Unproven, Research in Progress). Single-author coding, no second coder and no inter-rater reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The empirical data include altogether 128 fact-checking reports (for short, fact-checks) dealing with the Russo-Ukrainian conflict. The reports were published within the period of 24 February 2022-28 June 2023. The reports were identified from the website of Snopes.com using the search terms Russia AND Ukraine, and Ukraine AND war. All of the 128 fact-checks dealing with the above topic were downloaded for closer analysis.
estimates.notes: borderline=true because the denominator is the set of claims Snopes chose to check, so the share is driven by fact-checker selection (they check claims that are contested or suspected false) and cannot be read as prevalence in any population of content - the paper says as much: 'This suggests that the fact-checks tend to focus on claims that turn out to be invalid'. Kept because, unlike an all-false fact-check corpus, this one has a stated denominator and a genuine mix of verdicts (21.9% True, 7.8% Correct Attribution). The 54.7% is a sum of three Table 2 categories, but the author prints the summed figure verbatim in both the abstract and Section 5.1, so it is not a sum I computed. Year recorded as 2022, the start of a 24 Feb 2022 - 28 Jun 2023 window that straddles two years; there is no time series to collapse. Data are the reports as published, so no time-of-collection ambiguity beyond the publication window. platform_norm=web_cross_platform because Snopes checks claims wherever they surface (social-media images and videos, newspapers, television, government statements), not one platform.

estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: this is the strict-veracity reading of the same 128-report denominator whose broad reading gives the 54.7% row. Kept as a pair because the two together show how much of this corpus's 'invalidity' rests on miscaptioned authentic media (21.1 points of the 54.7) rather than fabricated claims - exactly the definitional lever the review is coding for. Same borderline caveat about the fact-check-selected denominator.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the remaining Table 2 categories individually (True 21.9, Miscaptioned 21.1, Correct attribution 7.8, Mixture 7.8, Research in progress 3.2, Labeled satire 2.3, Unproven 2.3, Outdated 1.6). The two rows above already span the strict and broad falsity definitions on this denominator; adding each category would multiply rows without adding an estimate, and the valid/mixed categories are not misinformation shares. (2) The 15.6% 'mixed' share - by construction it mixes valid and invalid elements, so it is neither a falsity share nor a truth share. (3) The evaluation-grounds distribution (Correctness of information 39.0%, Temporal compatibility 16.3%, Verifiability of an event 12.3%, ...) and the information-source distribution (e.g. Government 15.6%) - these describe the fact-checkers' reasoning and evidence, not the prevalence of false content. (4) Section 6's comparison with Vu et al. - a figure from another study, barred by R8. Internal inconsistency worth flagging: the abstract and Section 5.1 give the positive (valid) share as 26.7%, but Table 2's True (21.9) plus Correct attribution (7.8) is 29.7, which is the figure printed later at Section 5.3 ('more frequently rated as invalid (54.7%) than valid (29.7%)'). The 26.7% therefore looks like a typo. This does not touch either extracted row, both of which sit on the invalid side, but it is a reason to hold confidence at medium rather than high. Table 2's percentages also do not sum to exactly 100 in the reproduced text (32.0+21.9+21.1+7.8+7.8+3.2+2.3+2.3+1.6 = 100.0, which does close), and 54.7% of 128 = 70 items and 32.0% of 128 = 41 items, both consistent.

rob.design: Single-author descriptive quantitative plus qualitative content analysis. Sampling frame: Snopes.com's own published fact-checks, retrieved by site search on 'Russia AND Ukraine' and 'Ukraine AND war'; all 128 hits from 24 February 2022 to 28 June 2023 were analysed, so it is a census of that search rather than a sample of circulating claims. Veracity ratings were not produced by the author but taken over from Snopes' 20-category scale. The author's own coding (nine evaluation grounds, information-source types) was inductive, developed over two readings with iterative category emergence 'until there were no anomalies'; no second coder, no inter-rater reliability, no formal sampling justification beyond qualitative saturation. Reports ranged 330-1,840 words. The author explicitly limits generalisation: 'As the study concentrated on fact-checking dealing with political information about a specific issue, the findings cannot be extended to concern the fact-checking practices in other contexts.' The decisive risk for this review is denominator selection: the corpus is what a fact-checking organisation elected to investigate.
rob.item6_quote: (3) False. The primary elements of a claim are demonstrably false. ... (5) Miscaptioned. This rating is used with photographs and videos that are "real" (i.e. not the product, partially or wholly, of digital manipulation) but are nonetheless misleading because they are accompanied by explanatory material that falsely describes their origin, context, and/or meaning.
